source: Gick & Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer
finding: With an explicit hint, people use a military analogue to solve Duncker's radiation problem. Without a hint, few notice it.
numbers: About 75% convergence solutions with analogue plus hint vs under 10% for controls. About 30% with no hint after memorising the story. Authors estimate only a third or less of potential users noticed the analogy.
limits: Student samples; one target problem family. Authors assume a 10% base rate from several replications.
agent_relevance: O7 fires only when the schema is cued. Unaided analogy retrieval is rare, so the scaffold must make the agent look for a source, not wait for one.

source: Gick & Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer
finding: Two analogues beat one. Comparing two stories lets people write an abstract schema, and the schema predicts transfer.
numbers: Two-analog groups: 45% convergence solutions before hint vs 21% for one analogue; total 80% vs 53% (G2(1)=6.35 and 8.36). Schema quality: 91% of subjects with good schemas solved without a hint.
limits: Schema quality is correlational within the experiment. Typical figures quoted by authors: about 30% unprompted and 75% in total.
agent_relevance: Give O7 two or more analogues and ask for the shared abstract rule before mapping. This is the strongest human intervention found.

source: Gick & Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer
finding: Giving the learner an abstract principle and diagrams raised schema quality and transfer.
numbers: With-principle condition: 44% good schemas vs 10% in the comparison condition; two analogues plus diagrams 57% vs 37% unprompted and 92% vs 79% total (G2(1)=7.55, 6.66). Diagram-only subjects: 7% spontaneous.
limits: Later experiments with small cells; diagrams are specific to the radiation story.
agent_relevance: Typed mapping output and an explicit principle statement are cheap analogues of the principle and diagram aids.

source: Gick & Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer
finding: Similar and dissimilar analogues give similar schema-driven transfer, but surface-dissimilar sources hurt poor schema writers most.
numbers: Poor schema writers solved without a hint 44% with similar analogues vs 12% with dissimilar analogues; good schema writers did well either way.
limits: Single paper; schema scoring is a lower bound on learning, authors say.
agent_relevance: Far analogues are safe only after an abstract schema exists. Build the schema first.

source: Holyoak & Koh (1987) Surface and structural similarity in analogical transfer
finding: Both surface and structural similarity drive spontaneous retrieval of an analogue. Structure matters more once the analogy is pointed out.
numbers: Laser+fragile-glass source (high on both): 69% spontaneous convergence solutions to the radiation problem. Removing surface or structure each cut transfer; both removed: 13%. Noticing the analogy ranged from 88% to 13% across the four cells.
limits: Student sample; the two similarity factors were about equal in size and did not interact.
agent_relevance: Retrieval of far analogues will fail by default. Retrieve with relational description (structure), not surface words.

source: Holyoak & Koh (1987) Surface and structural similarity in analogical transfer
finding: Experiment 1 found substantial spontaneous transfer even after a delay of several days, partly answering the earlier pessimism.
numbers: Abstract-level result: substantial transfer with a delay of days between source and target. Authors note the earlier figure (30% unprompted; about 20% above base rate) in the radiation task.
limits: Exact Exp 1 rates not recorded.
agent_relevance: Analogue memory can survive delay; saved past solutions in a memory store are worth retrieving.

source: Needham & Begg (1991) Problem-oriented training promotes spontaneous analogical transfer
finding: Spontaneous transfer is common when people first try to solve the training problem before seeing its solution.
numbers: After problem-oriented training solution rates over 80%; after memory-oriented training over 60%; baseline about 5%. Advantage held at 15 min delay. Five experiments; Exp 5 had 142 subjects.
limits: Training analogues were simple insight problems and dilemmas. Attempts at solving nearly always failed, so the benefit came from process match, not from knowing the answer.
agent_relevance: Attempt the problem first, then read the analogue. A failed attempt still primes retrieval. Fits the productive-failure link.

source: Needham & Begg (1991) Problem-oriented training promotes spontaneous analogical transfer
finding: Story or problem format of the training material had no effect once processing mode was controlled; recall of the training passages favoured memory-oriented study.
numbers: Solution rates unaffected by form (about .755 vs similar); memory-oriented subjects had an equally large advantage on a recall task.
limits: Same five experiments.
agent_relevance: Retrieval and use trade off with memorising: study for solving, not for recall.

source: Spencer & Weisberg (1986) Context-dependent effects on analogical transfer (as summarised in a search result)
finding: Reported no transfer to the radiation problem when a delay or a change of context separated the source from the target.
numbers: No numbers read this session.
limits: Known only from a search snippet; not opened.
agent_relevance: Supports the view that context similarity, not analogy, often drives retrieval.

source: Student replication note of Gick & Holyoak 1983 (search result)
finding: A student power analysis called the original two-analogue effect small and underpowered.
numbers: Snippet states d=0.20 and 68% power with 143 participants (unverified).
limits: Snippet only, not opened, not peer reviewed. Treat as a lead.
agent_relevance: Effect sizes for the classic effect are not well pinned down; do not lean on them.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) matched or beat UCLA students on digit matrices and letter-string analogies with no examples.
numbers: Digit Matrices: human N=40; GPT-3 above human mean on all problem types (multiple choice OR=6.27, p=2.3e-8). Letter strings: human N=57; GPT-3 OR=1.76, p=6.3e-5, driven by zero-generalization problems. Accuracy fell with more generalizations in both (GPT-3 OR=0.51).
limits: Authors admit letter-string problems may be on the web. Students, not a general population.
agent_relevance: Frontier models can do simple relational mapping on familiar formats, so O7 can use the model to map, but check by code.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: On story analogies, students beat GPT-3; GPT-4 did far better in a preliminary test.
numbers: Story analogy task: human N=54, 15 of 54 chose the analogous story on every trial; GPT-3 vs humans OR=0.37, p=0.0003. GPT-4 nearly perfect in near analogy and strong in far.
limits: GPT-4 test was preliminary and small.
agent_relevance: Natural-language analogy of causal structure was the weak spot for weaker models; stronger models closed the gap.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 results depended on prompt format.
numbers: Without the prompt, or in sentence form, letter-string performance dropped but stayed within the human range (within one SD) in several cases, and pattern across problem types still correlated with humans (r=0.76 for sentence format, p=4.2e-6).
limits: Supplementary analysis.
agent_relevance: Prompt framing matters for relational tasks. Fix a format and test the scaffold under two.

source: Hodel & West (2023) Response: Emergent analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: GPT-3 fails simple variants of the letter-string tasks while humans stay high. Zero-shot cannot be claimed without ruling out training overlap.
numbers: Authors ran a human behavioural check; humans stayed high on all modified versions; GPT-3 dropped (exact figures are in the appendix and were not extracted).
limits: A short critique; numbers sit in an appendix not read in detail. The original authors replied that the failure was counting.
agent_relevance: Do not trust a model's analogy score on public formats; test with altered, counterfactual surface forms.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Counterfactual alphabets (permuted or symbols) keep humans high and drop GPT-3, 3.5 and 4. A general ability did not replicate.
numbers: Mean accuracy over all alphabets and problem types: humans 0.753 (1,876 samples), GPT-3 0.488, GPT-3.5 0.350, GPT-4 0.452 (6,840 samples each). Humans stay flat as more letters are permuted; GPT falls. Counterfactual comprehension checks were mostly 0.9 to 1.0, so models understood the new alphabet.
limits: Prolific sample. Table order read from PDF text, labels may be shifted by one cell.
agent_relevance: The same model can pass a familiar task and fail a re-skinned twin. O7 mapping needs a code-checked verification step.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Error types differ: models often apply a different valid rule.
numbers: Share of errors from using an alternate rule: GPT-3 5.81%, GPT-4 22%, GPT-3.5 38.59%; humans about 15% in the same category.
limits: Error coding by the authors; small bins.
agent_relevance: Ambiguity of the rule is a failure source. Make the agent list candidate rules and test each on the given pairs.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2024) Evidence from counterfactual tasks supports emergent analogical reasoning in LLMs (reply)
finding: GPT-4 with code execution matched humans on counterfactual letter-string tasks. The failure was in counting positions, not in analogy.
numbers: Humans N=99 (interval 1) and N=97 (interval 2). Humans beat plain GPT-4 (P=8.9e-13); GPT-4 plus code execution matched humans (P=0.496).
limits: Reply by the original authors. Using code to count is not a human-like route.
agent_relevance: Offload exact index and counting steps to code in O7 and O6. A competing explanation that fits the scaffold design.

source: Stevenson, Pafford, van der Maas & Mitchell (2025) Can LLMs generalize analogy solving like children can?
finding: Children (7-9) and adults transfer letter-string rules from Latin to Greek and symbol alphabets; LLMs do not.
numbers: 42 children aged 7-9, 62 adults, several LLMs. Child accuracy in the reported table row stayed about 0.62 to 0.67 across domains; LLMs fell in the far symbol set.
limits: Exact LLM figures not extracted. Letter strings are one task type.
agent_relevance: The gap is in cross-domain transfer, exactly what O7 asks for. Do not assume far transfer.

source: Musker et al. (2025) LLMs as models for analogical reasoning
finding: Advanced LLMs match humans in several conditions on mapping words to letter or symbol sequences, but respond differently to semantic distractors.
numbers: Humans compared with GPT-4, Claude 3 and Llama-405B. They matched humans across several conditions. Humans mostly ignored the distractor; models were pulled by it (counts not recorded).
limits: Abstract and result headings read; per-condition numbers not recorded.
agent_relevance: Irrelevant semantic content is a risk. Strip surface content before mapping (O6 then O7).

source: Sourati et al. (2024) ARN: Analogical Reasoning on Narratives
finding: LLMs spot near analogies but fail far analogies between stories; GPT-4 scored below chance on far analogies zero-shot.
numbers: Humans: 97.9% near, 94.1% far. Models: 75.0% near, 39.6% far on average (random 50%).
limits: Binary task built from proverb-labeled narratives. Structured guidance helped (gain in abstract, not recorded).
agent_relevance: Far analogies are where gain is largest and failure is worst. Use typed element mappings, not free recall.

source: Sourati et al. (2024) ARN: Analogical Reasoning on Narratives
finding: Surface overlap pulls models away from system mappings.
numbers: Models scored 33.9% when picking a far analogy over a surface-similar distractor; 73.2% average near vs near; 76.9% choosing near analogy over far disanalogy.
limits: Same benchmark.
agent_relevance: Surface-similar distractors are the main trap for any retrieval step.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners
finding: Asking the model to recall relevant problems before solving beats 0-shot CoT and manual few-shot CoT on average.
numbers: Average gain +4% across GSM8K, MATH, Codeforces and BIG-Bench with GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4, PaLM2 and text-davinci. Codeforces: self-generated knowledge plus exemplars added gains over exemplars alone.
limits: Row labels in extracted tables are scrambled, so single cells are uncertain. Costs more tokens.
agent_relevance: Cheap self-generated analogues help strong models.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners
finding: Scale is a boundary condition: with small LLMs retrieved exemplars beat self-generated ones.
numbers: Sweep from text-curie-001 to text-davinci-003 on GSM8K: analogical prompting beat 0-shot and 0-shot CoT at all scales, but retrieved CoT was better with smaller models.
limits: One vendor family and era.
agent_relevance: Gate O7 by model strength; fall back to retrieved examples for weak models.

source: Yu et al. (2024) Thought Propagation: an analogical approach to complex reasoning with LLMs
finding: Solve analogous easier problems first and reuse their solutions to fix the first answer.
numbers: Abstract: +12% absolute optimal-solution rate in shortest-path, +13% human preference in creative writing, +15% task completion in agent planning. 1-layer TP costs about the same tokens as ToT; 2 layers cost more.
limits: Only abstract and cost section skimmed. Baselines are the authors' own.
agent_relevance: A candidate for making O7 productive: one layer of analogues, not deep.

source: Si, Yang & Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas?
finding: Blind expert review found LLM ideas more novel than expert-written ideas, slightly less feasible.
numbers: 49 idea writers; 79 reviewers; 298 unique reviews. Mean novelty: human 4.84, AI 5.64, AI plus human rerank 5.81 (p<0.05, Welch tests).
limits: NLP topics, text ideas, not executed projects.
agent_relevance: Use outside judges for ideas; novelty is real but feasibility lags.

source: Si, Yang & Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas?
finding: LLM idea generation lacks diversity and LLM self-evaluation is weak.
numbers: Only about 5% of generated seed ideas were non-duplicate after similarity filtering. Claude-3.5-Sonnet predicted accepted papers at 71.4%; GPT-4o 61.1%; Claude-3-Opus 63.5%.
limits: Same study.
agent_relevance: Overgenerate then dedupe hard; never let the generator pick its own best idea (matches G8).

source: Franceschelli & Musolesi (2025) On the creativity of large language models
finding: Using Boden's three kinds (combinatorial, exploratory, transformational), LLMs fit the first two and probably not the third.
numbers: No experiment. Authors argue transformational creativity is not reachable by current LLM training and may need other architectures.
limits: Conceptual review.
agent_relevance: Combinatorial and exploratory creativity can be scaffolded; do not expect the model to break its own frame without O8-type reframing.

source: Padmakumar & He (2024) Does writing with language models reduce content diversity?
finding: Writing with InstructGPT, not base GPT-3, cut diversity across authors. Suggestions were less diverse; human text unchanged.
numbers: 38 Upwork writers across three groups (solo, GPT-3, InstructGPT). Significant drop in lexical and content diversity only with InstructGPT.
limits: Argumentative essays, one task, small sample.
agent_relevance: Feedback-tuned models narrow output. For idea search, sample wide or vary prompts and sources.
